content: The combination of artesunate and mefloquine has been evaluated as a treatment for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, particularly in regions with low malaria transmission and high resistance to single-drug therapies. This review compared the efficacy of artesunate plus mefloquine versus mefloquine alone. The primary outcome assessed was treatment failure by day 28, defined as the presence of parasitaemia with or without clinical symptoms between the start of treatment (day 0) and day 28. Eight randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials, involving a total of 1,996 participants, were included in the analysis. These trials were conducted in areas with low malaria transmission, with seven studies performed in South-East Asia and one in the Peruvian Amazon. The dosing regimens of artesunate and mefloquine varied across the trials. However, trials that used a total dose of 25 mg/kg of mefloquine combined with 10 mg of artesunate consistently demonstrated fewer treatment failures at all time points. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) for treatment failure at day 28 was 0.17 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.06 to 0.47) based on data from 824 participants across four trials. At day 42, the RR was 0.23 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.39) from one trial involving 298 participants, and at day 63, the RR was 0.26 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.77) from two trials involving 501 participants. These results indicate a significant reduction in treatment failure rates with the combination therapy compared to mefloquine alone. The findings for parasitaemia followed a similar trend, favoring the combination therapy. Trials that used lower doses of artesunate also tended to show better outcomes with the combination therapy compared to mefloquine monotherapy, although the effect was less pronounced. Adverse events were reported to be similar across both treatment groups, suggesting that the combination therapy does not increase the risk of side effects. The authors concluded that artesunate plus mefloquine is more effective than mefloquine alone for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in areas with low malaria transmission. A total dose of 25 mg/kg of mefloquine combined with at least 10 mg of artesunate is associated with higher cure rates. They also emphasized the need for better reporting of study methods and standardization of outcomes to improve the interpretation of future research. As of 2008, the World Health Organization no longer recommends monotherapy for malaria treatment. Consequently, the authors do not intend to update this review.
